All of salvation history is commemorated yet again in services of each day.
The Church follows Chaldean (Biblical) time for commemorations
The day begins at sunset with Vespers
The Church follows Roman time for fasting (The day begins at midnight).
The daily cycle of services parallel the Temple services, which took place every three hours and in which tradition the Apostles participated (Acts 3:1; 10:9)
These constitute the full schedule of services that can be prayed each day:
Vespers
Evening Prayer: Inaugurates the beginning of the new day (at the setting of the sun).
Theme: creation, sin and fall from God, and salvation in Christ.
Compline
“Bed Time” prayers (“Grant, O Master, when we depart to sleep…”
Theme: Repentance, thanksgiving, cry of deliverance from evil and darkness.
Midnight Office
“Morning Prayers,” a glorification of God before sunrise
Theme: Praising God for His revelation (Ps 118) and petition for grace
Orthros/Matins
Theme: Repentance, expulsion from paradise, Resurrection (Sunday) and glorification of God
The main morning service, and commemorations of the day
First Hour (6:00am): Pss. 5, 89, 100 (LXX)
Theme: The light of new day and the light of God’s commandments
Third Hour (9:00am): Pss. 16, 24, 50 (LXX)
Prayer at the time of the coming of the Holy Spirit (Pentecost)
Theme: righteousness and wisdom vs. iniquity and foolishness
Sixth Hour (12:00 noon): 53, 54, 90 (LXX)
Prayer at the time of Christ’s crucifixion
Theme: adversity, temptation to despair, deliverance
Ninth Hour (3:00pm): 83, 84, 85
The last service of the day (sometimes held directly before Vespers)
Theme: Christ’s saving death on the Cross
[v] A Brief Introduction to the Divine Liturgy
The Divine Liturgy is the central Eucharistic Celebration of the Orthodox Church.
Technically speaking, it is not part of the daily cycle of services.
It transcends time and makes present Christ’s work of salvation in the here and now.
It touches the heavenly realm, uniting the earthly with the heavenly (Eph. 1:10).
“Liturgy” means “common work” of, or for, the people
A priest cannot celebrate alone
There must be “Lord have mercy” and an “Amen” from the laity
Not merely prayer, but a corporate act and offering
“Do this in remembrance of Me” (Lk. 22:19; 1 Cor. 11:24)
“Eucharist”: our “thanksgiving” to God
“Divine” refers to the work of the Holy Trinity
Jesus is Celebrant: “the one who offers and is offered.”
He offers to the Father, who sends the Holy Spirit
The Liturgy makes the entire life and work of Christ present to us.
The Life of Christ – infancy, public ministry, sacrifice, Resurrection,
Ascension, sitting at right hand, second coming
The Pentecostal descent of the Spirit, which founded the Church.
His servants, the angels and saints, worship with us (Heb. 12:22-24)
The Holy Gifts become truly the Body and Blood of Christ by the Holy Spirit.
The Structure of the Divine Liturgy
The Divine Liturgy has three main sections:
[i] The Proskomedia (“Liturgy of Preparation” – done privately by the priest)

The bread and wine are prepared with the following themes:. The mystery hidden from all eternity (Col 1:26). The lamb slain from the foundation of the world (Rev 13:8). The nativity of Christ (Mt 2:9)
. The Creation of the world (Ps 93:1)
. The manifestation of the Church (Ps 45:9)
[ii] Liturgy of the Catechumens (fulfillment of synagogue worship)
“Blessed is the Kingdom” – the beginning of the public ministry of Christ
Kinship with Synagogue worship
Hymns of Praise: Psalms and Hymns
Little Entrance (entering with Gospel and the angels)
Trisagion (angelic hymn)
Climax: Communion with the Word of God through Epistle/Gospel readings
Didactic: The Sermon
Prayers for and dismissal of catechumens
[iii] Liturgy of the Faithful/Eucharist (fulfillment of Temple sacrifices)
The Cherubic Hymn (Heavenly worship; “Lay aside all earthly cares”)
The Great Entrance (offering our Gifts)
Unity of Love and Faith: “Let us love one another” and Creed

The Anaphora (“Offering”): The heart of the Liturgy. The anamnesis (remembrance) of God’s economy,. Prayers of Thanksgiving,. Words of Institution. Invocation and Consecration. Commemoration of all the faithful
The Lord’s Prayer
The Fracture: “Holy Things for the holy”
Pre-Communion Prayers (partaking worthily)
Holy Communion with Christ through His Body and Blood
“Let us depart in peace” (the “liturgy after the Liturgy”)
Key Points and Practical Applications for our Life in Christ
Woven through the cycles of fasts and feasts of the Liturgical year of the Orthodox Church is Christ Himself, manifested in the lives of His saints and the events of His life.
Participation in this life forms Christ in us, from his birth to His Passion and Resurrection, bringing us step by step into the full stature of the perfect man.
From the Fathers
“Communion, then, is God’s union with us, our deification, sanctification, fullness of grace, enlightenment, prevention of everything against us, and granting of every good.

What else is both a commingling and communion with God? This is the mystery of mysteries, the sanctification of saints, truly the holy of holies, the rite of all rites, both the beginning author and final completion of the rites. Since the originator of the rite, the Word, alone established it and passed it on, He Himself is the rite; and in order that He remain with us, He has passed it on.” – St Symeon of Thessalonika, On the Sacred Liturgy, c. 6.

lessons.title: The Liturgical Cycles of Worship

lessons.synopsis: In the Orthodox Church, iconography and church architecture bear witness to the reality of the Kingdom of God on earth and the Lord’s Presence with us in our worship. Icons are not only permissible in worship but spiritually necessary because God Himself in Christ has become visible and dwelt among us. Therefore, we can depict Him, His Beloved Mother, and the Saints and Angels who gather to worship with us to provide us with the reality of the Kingdom of Heaven in our midst

blocks.text: [i] The Physical Arrangement of an Orthodox Church
The Scriptures present two perspectives of God’s presence in the world:
First, God “does not dwell in temples made by hands” (Acts 17:24).
He is everywhere present and fills all things
“Where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 139:7).
Second, God is personally manifest in holy places of His choosing
Burning bush (Ex 3:5); Joshua (Joshua 5:15); Jacob (Gen 28:17)
“And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying… let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them” (Ex 25:1, 8).
God is both transcendent and immanent simultaneously.
There two main features of the architectural layout of an Orthodox Church incorporate these two Biblical perspectives:
First, the dome over the central nave.
God is equally with us at all stages of our life, from the back of the Church to the Altar
Second, the separation of the sanctuary by the iconostasis and curtain
God is personally manifest in consecrated space, made holy unto Him
The presence of heaven
The veil conceals and reveals heaven. As did the veil of the flesh of Christ (Heb 6:19; 10:20)
. Heaven by definition is ineffable and must be sought The structure of an Orthodox church has three main areas: Sanctuary, Nave, Narthex
This structure is similar to the Tabernacle revealed to Moses
The first day of creation: the Holy of Holies, the noetic, heavenly, angelic realm
The second day of creation: the firmament, the veil; etc.
St Maximus the Confessor (Mystagogia, chs. 1-5). likens the structure to that of the world and the human being
Sanctuary is the nous, the altar being the heart of man
The nave, the soul
The narthex, the body
The Church is thus a microcosm of the world redeemed, and the human being a temple of God (1 Cor 3:16)
The one High Priest is the same for all three liturgies: Christ
In the world, as Logos
In the human heart, from baptism
In the temple, as the officiant of every Liturgy, the “Offerer and Offered”
The Structure of the Orthodox temple is thus a fulfillment of the revelation to Moses; a microcosm of the world as it is meant to be; and a path back to paradise.
[ii] Icons
Early Church Art and Symbols
Virgin Mary by St. Luke
Holy Napkin – some believe to be the Shroud of Turin
Iconoclasts – Who were they?
The Orthodox Response:
St. John of Damascus
St. Theodore the Studite
Seventh Ecumenical Council
The Sunday of the Triumph of Orthodoxy
The Theology of the Icon
Worship vs. Veneration
Concept of Presence
Dogmatic essence: a Confession that God became truly man
The Necessity of Icons in Worship
Explanation of Icons and their Placement
Icon of Christ
Icon of the Theotokos
Selected Feast-day Icons Explained
The Use of Color and facial features
Other Symbols in Icons
Key Points and Practical Applications for our Life in Christ

“Standing in the Temple of Thy Glory, We Think Ourselves to Stand in Heaven, O Theotokos.” While on the one hand we are children in our Father’s house, enjoying the liberty of the children of God, on the other hand, the holiness of the church temple should inspire us to piety and respect.
Appropriate dress
Shows reverence to God and respect towards our fellow worshippers
Should always be becoming of a Christian
We offer Christ our best
Shorts, tank-tops, immodest dress, or shirts with writing are not appropriate Entering the Temple
We should make the sign of the Cross, venerate the icons
Refrain from speech by greeting others with a nod and smile
Arrive on time
One should not receive Communion if late for the Scripture Readings
Conduct in Church
Have a reverent attitude and demeanor at all times in Church
Be patient and loving to all
Do not cross legs, chew gum or talk during the Divine Liturgy
Receiving Holy Communion
Be a faithful, practicing Orthodox Christian
Prepare by reading the pre-Communion prayers at home, fasting from midnight, and repentance/confession
Approach the chalice with reverence, arms crossed and one’s mind on Christ Leaving the Temple
Reverently, making the Cross
From the Fathers

“Christ, the Lord’s sheep is sacrificed; when you hear the words, “Let us pray” when you behold the curtains drawn up, then imagine that the Heavens are let down from above, and that the Angels are descending!” – St John Chrysostom, Homily 3 in Ephesians (NPNF 1.13, p.64)

For this holy altar, too, by which I stand, is stone, ordinary in its nature, nowise different from the other slabs of stone that build our houses and adorn our pavements; but seeing that it was consecrated to the service of God, and received the benediction, it is a holy table, an altar undefiled, no longer touched by the hands of all, but of the priests alone, and that with reverence. – St Gregory of Nyssa, On the Baptism of Christ (NPNF 2.05, p. 175).

“For he entered the Church attended by the whole of his train; it was the festival of the Epiphany, and the Church was crowded, and, by taking his place among the people, he made a profession of unity.... Upon his entrance he was struck by the thundering roll of the Psalms, by the sea of heads of the congregation, and by the angelic rather than human order which pervaded the sanctuary and its precincts…” – St Gregory the Theologian (describing the Emperor Valens entering the church of St Basil), Funeral Oration for St Basil the Great, c. 52.

lessons.synopsis: God is wondrous in His saints! The Church on earth communes with the Church victorious in heaven and venerates the saints for the glorious work that God has accomplished in the world through them. They are not distant to us, but form one Body of the Church with the living. Hence, they are open to our supplications, and assist us in following the Lord.

blocks.text: [i] What is Sanctity?
Something is holy if [i] it is set apart for a sacred purpose, and [ii] manifests the presence of God’s uncreated grace and power.

Just as our churches are consecrated with chrism to be set apart as God’s temples, so is the same chrism used to mark the bodies of the newly baptized, setting them apart as God’s living temples (1 Cor 6:19).
[ii] What is a Saint?
Saints are those separated from the world (2 Cor 6:17; Jn 15:19), in order to be sanctified by the indwelling and operation of the Holy Spirit.
By striving to overcome our sinful desires and leave the harmful patterns of worldly life behind us, we become separate from the world (1 Jn 3:1).
The promise of our faith is the gift of the Spirit in Christ, and the life of the age to come.
Holiness, as incorruptible grace, is a gift of God.
Holiness is cultivated through our life in Christ, through the Sacraments, and following His teachings.
The first Christian saints were martyrs.
Through their suffering, martyrs bear witness to their hidden life with Christ.
All the other kinds of saints, in their own way, imitate the martyric ideal.
All Christians are called by God to be saints (Rom 1:7; 1 Cor 1:2)
The Church recognizes those distinguished by their exceptional holiness, witness to the Gospel, and power of intercession as canonized saints.
This recognition helps believers recognize and imitate authentic sanctity.
The canonized saints do not exhaust the choir of saints known to God alone.
[iii] The Communion of Saints

All those who share in the life of Christ are united in fellowship, both here on earth and in heaven (Heb 12:22-24). The saints in heaven do not cease being conscious because they are truly alive in Christ (Lk 20:29040; Rev 6:9-10).
The Christians still living on earth are called the Church Militant because we are still striving to battle the world, the flesh, and the devil.
Christians in heaven (the saints) are the Church Triumphant because they have finished their part of the struggle.

“We live together with them (the Saints in heaven) in the House of the Heavenly Father, only in di55fferent parts of it. We live in the earthly, they in the heavenly half; but we can Converse with them and they with us” (St. John of Kronstadt).
We gather with the Theotokos, the angelic hosts, and all the Saints (living and departed) to worship the Holy Trinity.
[iv] The Cult of the Saints
The saints, as the friends of God, have the ability to pray for us.
“The effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much” (James 5:16)
The intercession of the Saints bring about a great reversal in irreversible situations.
Abraham prays for Abimalech (Gen 20)
Job prays for his two friends (Job 42:7-9)
Elisha raises the Shunnamite woman’s son (2 Kings 4)
Moses prays for the people (Num 11:2; 12:13; 21:7)
We ask the saints for their intercessions, guidance, and protection, especially our patron saints and guardian angels.
The veneration we give the saints is distinct from the divine adoration we owe to God alone.
The Greek word “Latria” means sacrificial worship: only for God.
The Greek word “Dulia” means a veneration of honor.
Both God and everything consecrated to God (saints, Bible, icons, etc.) deserve reverence.
We honor the saints in various ways: celebrate feast days, go on pilgrimages to shrines, venerate icons, light candles, lamps, and incense.
Instead of admiring worldly heroes or vain celebrities, Christians should venerate spiritual heroes.
The reality of the saints is a fulfilment of man’s original vocation to be the image of God, manifesting God’s presence in the world.
What about 1 Timothy 2:5?

“First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life, godly and respectful in every way. This is good, and it is acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
Does the cult of the Saints nullify the fact that Jesus is the one mediator?
Absolutely not! No one substitutes for Christ.
. All the Saints lead us to Christ.
. The Head is always with His body, the Church (that is, the Saints)
We come not only to God, but to the assembly of Saints in heaven as well.
“We also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (literally, “martyrs”) (Heb 12:1).

“But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn who are registered in heaven, to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of just men made perfect, to Jesus the Mediator of the new covenant” (Heb 12:22-24).
. Paul says we come directly not only to God, but to an assembly of Saints in heaven (the just men made perfect) exactly in the context of Jesus being the mediator!
[v] Relics of Saints
We venerate the relics of the saints as reminders of the reality of the bodily Resurrection.
A testimony to the abiding, incorruptible grace in the Saint: the body remains a temple of the Holy Spirit even after death
Biblical: Elisha’s bones resurrected dead (2 Kings 13:21); napkins touched to St Paul’s body healed people (Acts 19:11-12); St Peter’s shadow (Acts 5:15).
Veneration of relics dates back to the early Church (Martyrdom of Polycarp, cc. 17-18)
Key Points and Practical Applications for our Life in Christ
We need the Saints. Not just their examples, as in a book.
We need the power of their prayers, their energy, their wisdom, their unconquerable faith, their unwavering love for Christ, and their patient guidance.
The Saints are alive.
They are not distant from us, but pray with us, and pray for us.
They assist us to live in and for Christ, such that we too can be sanctified.
In short, the Saints love us.

“Through his self-offering to Christ, through his communion with Christ, and through Christ, with all men, the saint restores his humanity completely … He has become simple, because he has surrendered himself entirely to God. That is why he can surrender himself entirely to others” – Dumitru Stăniloae, The Experience of God, vol. 1, pp. 234-5.

“Belief in the deification of the body and in its eventual resurrection helps to explain the Orthodox veneration of relics. Since the body is redeemed and sanctified along with soul, and since the body will rise again, it is only fitting that Christians should show respect for the bodily remains of the saints. Reverence for relics is not the fruit of ignorance and superstition, but springs from a highly developed theology of the body” (Kallistos Ware, quoted in Coniaris, Introducing the Orthodox Church, p. 103).
From the Fathers

“How the Creator and Provider of all has honored and adorned our nature! The saints shine with His light; they are hallowed by His grace, having conquered sin and washed away every impurity of body and spirit; they are glorious with His glory; they are incorruptible through His incorruption. Glory to God, Who has so honored, enlightened, and exalted our nature.”
– St. John of Kronstadt, The Spiritual Counsels.

“Though the soul is not present, a power resides in the bodies of the saints because of the righteous soul which has for many years dwelt in it, or used it as its minister” (St. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures, XVIII, 16).
